summary: This document specifies how a Source Address Validation Improvement (SAVI) device binds a DHCPv4 or DHCPv6-assigned IP address to a binding anchor. Those bindings are used to filter packets with forged source addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: If the network gave you a particular seat, it can check that messages claiming to be from that seat really come from there.

questions: prevent ip spoofing with dhcp snooping
how does dhcp snooping stop ip spoofing
what is the binding state table
subtitle: How a switch learns, from DHCP traffic, which address belongs to which port and drops packets that lie about their source.

tldr.problem: Hosts can send packets with forged source IP addresses, which enables amplification attacks, and ingress filtering at network borders cannot stop a host from spoofing another host inside the same network.
tldr.mechanism: A SAVI device watches DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 exchanges and records a binding between each assigned address and a binding anchor such as a switch port. It then discards packets whose source address does not match a binding on the attachment they came from. An optional data-triggered process recovers bindings that DHCP snooping missed.
tldr.outcome: Address-granularity source validation inside a network, complementing BCP 38 (RFC 2827) prefix-granularity filtering. It does not cover stateless DHCP or SLAAC addresses.

today: RFC 7513 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It sits alongside RFC 6620, which the text points to for SLAAC and link-local addresses.

sections.title: Source Address Validation for DHCP
sections.content:
This RFC describes a fine-grained check on the source addresses of IPv4 and IPv6 packets. A SAVI device (usually a switch) creates bindings between addresses handed out by DHCP and a binding anchor, a property that is immutable or hard to change and that identifies the system, such as a switch port or a Wi-Fi security association. Packets from that attachment with any other source address are filtered. Forging source addresses is called spoofing, and it is key to amplification attacks.

BCP 38 (RFC 2827) protects a network from a neighboring network by checking prefixes. SAVI-DHCP protects a network, including a LAN, from itself by checking individual addresses when DHCP assigns them.

Scope is deliberate. It is designed for stateful DHCP (RFC 2131, RFC 3315). Stateless DHCP is out of scope, and hosts using SLAAC should use FCFS SAVI (RFC 6620). Link-local addresses are not blocked, and the RFC RECOMMENDS a separate SAVI solution for them. DHCP address assignment in IPv4/IPv6 transition scenarios is also out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a school where each kid is told which desk is theirs. A teacher then checks that notes passed out of a desk really say they came from the kid sitting there.

sections.title: Attributes and the Protection Perimeter
sections.content:
Each attachment point on a SAVI device carries Boolean attributes that say what to do with traffic from it. Trust means packets need not be validated, as for a port to another SAVI device or a router; it defaults to FALSE. DHCP-Trust means the attached device may send DHCP Server-to-Client messages, as a DHCP server or relay does; it defaults to FALSE. DHCP-Snooping means client messages on that attachment create bindings. Data-Snooping means data packets may trigger binding setup, and should default to FALSE. Validating means source addresses are checked, and by default is the inverse of Trust.

Some pairs are mutually exclusive and MUST NOT both be TRUE on one attachment: Trust excludes DHCP-Snooping, Data-Snooping and Validating. Setting Validating FALSE with snooping TRUE is the expected way to monitor forged traffic without blocking it. By default a SAVI switch filters nothing until SAVI-DHCP is enabled.

The attributes build a perimeter. Validating and DHCP-Snooping go on client attachments, Trust on links to other SAVI devices, and DHCP-Trust on links to trusted DHCP relays and servers. Trusted DHCP servers and relays must sit inside the perimeter, because server replies arriving across it are not trusted. A bogus server and a valid server outside the perimeter look the same to the SAVI device.

The mechanism is only as strong as its anchor. A SAVI device MUST use a non-spoofable and exclusive binding anchor. If a protected non-SAVI device such as a desktop switch sits between the host and the SAVI device, a port alone is insufficient and something like a MAC address SHOULD be added.
sections.plainLanguage: Each door in the building gets a label: trusted guest, kitchen staff, or ordinary student. The guards then know whose notes to check and whose to let through.

sections.title: The Binding State Table
sections.content:
Bindings live in the Binding State Table (BST), which may be central in the switch or spread across its ports. There is one entry for each IPv4 or IPv6 address of each binding anchor. Each entry has six fields: Anchor, Address, State, Lifetime (remaining seconds), TID (the DHCP transaction ID, used to match server messages to entries) and Timeouts (used only by the data snooping process).

The Identity Association is not stored, because each address in an IA is leased separately, it cannot be recovered through leasequery for data-triggered bindings, and DHCPv4 has no IA. A binding entry limit on each binding anchor stops a malicious or broken node from overloading the table.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a roster with six columns: which desk, which address, how far along the sign-up is, how long it lasts, a ticket number, and a count of tries.

sections.title: The DHCP Snooping Process
sections.content:
The idea is simple: if a client legitimately uses a DHCP address, the assignment must have passed through its attachment. This works when the SAVI device is a cut vertex, always on the path between the client and the DHCP servers or relays. There are three states: NO_BIND, INIT_BIND (a potential binding) and BOUND.

A DHCPv4 Request or Reboot, a DHCPv6 Request, a DHCPv6 Solicit with Rapid Commit, or a DHCPv6 Confirm creates an entry in INIT_BIND with a lifetime of MAX_DHCP_RESPONSE_TIME. A successful DHCPv4 ACK or DHCPv6 Reply moves it to BOUND with a lifetime of the lease time plus MAX_DHCP_RESPONSE_TIME. For a Reply answering a Confirm, which may carry no lease time, the device SHOULD send a leasequery or else MUST set a preconfigured DHCP_DEFAULT_LEASE. Decline and Release messages remove the entry, and so does lifetime expiry.

A message only counts if it passes checks: attribute, destination, binding anchor, transaction ID, binding limit and address checks. A message that triggers no valid event is still forwarded if it passes the control packet filtering rules.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for a seat, you are first marked as maybe. Once the office confirms it, you are marked as sitting there. If the confirmation never comes, the mark is erased.

sections.title: The Data Snooping Process
sections.content:
DHCP snooping fails when there are multiple paths and the SAVI device is not on all of them, or when the path changes, for example after a host moves to another switch port without redoing DHCP. The Data Snooping Process avoids permanently blocking legitimate traffic in these cases. It is OPTIONAL because snooping data traffic burdens the processor of the SAVI device. It SHOULD be enabled unless the deployment is known to avoid these cases, such as tree topologies without host movement.

It does not act on every unmatched packet. The device decides probabilistically, and successive triggers on one attachment MUST be at least DATA_SNOOPING_INTERVAL apart. When it acts, it creates an entry in DETECTION and checks for a duplicate address with ARP or Neighbor Solicitation. It then moves to RECOVERY and sends DHCP leasequeries (RFC 4388, RFC 5007) to authorized servers. After a lease is found it moves to VERIFY and checks, by ARP or Neighbor Solicitation, that the attached device really holds the address. IPv4 also compares the hardware address from the leasequery with the ARP Reply. Success makes the entry BOUND.

Each step is sent over an unreliable path, so it is tried twice with a timeout before the entry is given up and deleted. A conflict reply from another attachment deletes it at once. The packet that triggered the process SHOULD be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: If the office never saw you get your seat, the guard asks around: is anyone else using this address, did the office really give it out, and is it really you? Only then do you get to send notes.

sections.title: Filtering and State Restoration
sections.content:
Data packets from an attachment with Validating TRUE MUST have their source address validated. A packet with a non-link-local source and no matching BOUND entry MUST be discarded, though it may trigger the Data Snooping Process if that attribute is set. With Validating FALSE, packets are forwarded unchecked. The device MAY log failures.

Control packets (DHCP, ARP and Neighbor Discovery) have their own rules. For example, DHCPv4 client messages must have source address all zeros or a bound address, and DHCP Server-to-Client messages from attachments without DHCP-Trust or Trust MUST be discarded.

After a reboot, attribute configuration MUST be kept in non-volatile storage, because without it the function cannot work. Restoring bindings from non-volatile storage is RECOMMENDED, since recovering many bindings by data snooping is heavy and slow. Entries that would already have expired MUST be removed.
sections.plainLanguage: The guard lets notes through only if the address matches the roster. After a power cut, a saved copy of the roster means nobody has to be re-checked from scratch.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Data snooping is costly and an attacker can trigger it by sending data packets, so it MUST be rate limited by DATA_SNOOPING_INTERVAL. It can also set up an incorrect binding if the real holder of an address does not answer the probes, since a leasequery only shows that an address is assigned, not to whom.

Leasequeries from SAVI devices MUST follow the securing recommendations in RFC 4388 and RFC 5007, which recommends IPsec. When a client leaves, the device starts a timer of OFFLINK_DELAY on its bindings, cancelling it if the client returns. Indirect client departures are not noticed, so switches supporting indirect attachment SHOULD use client-specific information such as a MAC address in the anchor.

The RFC says the mechanism cannot be perfectly compatible with Detecting Network Attachment (DNA), because it does not set up bindings from DNA probes, which slows reconfiguration but does not prevent it. On privacy, a SAVI device MUST delete binding anchor information as soon as the address state is back to NO_BIND, unless it is likely to help trace actual spoofing, and information about hosts that never spoof SHOULD NOT be logged.
sections.plainLanguage: The roster must not be flooded with fake sign-ups, and the guard should forget who sat where as soon as it no longer matters.
